title: The Heritage Wish List for the 118th Congress
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene reads the Heritage Foundation's education wish list for the incoming Congress as a preview of what will be lobbied hard in the coming session. He walks through its early childhood, K-12 and higher-education planks, conceding a point on household-employee child care taxes before turning sharply critical. His central claim is that the list is a consistent push toward vouchers, portable federal funds, private lending and loosely sponsored accreditation that would wear down publicly funded services. He also catches rhetorical inconsistencies, such as objecting to compelled speech while proposing gag laws on classroom topics. Characteristically, he uses wry commentary rather than data to expose what he sees as privatization by incremental steps. The piece fits Practice & Culture as Greene's school-policy commentary.
points: Greene treats the Heritage list as a lobbying preview, so the policy items matter more than the party label on them.
He grants that the household-employee child care tax burden is a real problem for lower-income families, which shows his critique is selective rather than reflexive.
Proposals to make IDEA and Title I funds portable and to extend ESA-style vouchers to military and tribal students are framed as incremental voucher footholds.
He points out the tension in invoking compelled speech while recommending bans on teaching certain ideas in DC schools.
His higher-education reading is that private accreditation and the end of federal loans would suit privateers but not ordinary students.
quotes: But this is a list we should pay attention to, because it's what the next Congress is going to get lobbied hard for. So let's see what these folks want to find under their tree next year.

I actually don't entirely disagree with their very first item, which is a safe harbor for household employee child care. Currently, if you are spending more than $2,400 for a sitter/nanny in your home, you are required to do all those employer things like withholding taxes and submitting quarterly payments to the IRS and I know rich folks who have inhouse nannies could just suck it up, but I know a few not-rich people for whom this stuff is a real issue.

Remember the 529 savings programs that let parents "invest" money for college funds. Back in 2017, Congress expanded the program so that it can now be used to pay for K-12 expenses like private school tuition.

And in the continuing attempt to get voucher feet in the door, Heritage would like Congress to make IDEA and Title I funds "portable," as vouchers for things like micro-education savings accounts. While we're at it, says Heritage, lets also institute federal vouchers (education savings account style) for military families and students on tribal lands.

When Congress gets back to work, look for these choice ideas to crop up, as Heritage continues its tradition at whittling away at any kind of taxpayer-funded services for other people in hopes that someday there will be nothing left but a sliver that rich folks can use to pick at their own teeth. Here's hoping Santa decides they've been very naughty.
